s0: Calgary. A city of big skies, with the Rocky Mountains on its doorstep.
How far could tourism here really go?
Here is what the numbers say.
s1: In twenty twenty-five, Calgary welcomed ten and a half million visitors.
They spent three point three billion dollars.
Hotels were sixty-seven and a half percent full.
And tourism and hospitality supported eighty-four thousand jobs.
s2: So where does that money come from?
One billion dollars comes from Albertans, and one point two billion from the rest of Canada.
Visitors from the United States and overseas add just over one billion more.
Put together, about two dollars in every three come from Canadians, and one in three from abroad.
And that international share is growing. In the first quarter of twenty twenty-six, international visitor spending rose more than fifteen percent.
s3: Calgary's airport handled nineteen point four million passengers in twenty twenty-five.
It flies non-stop to one hundred and ten destinations.
Fifteen new routes were added in a single year.
And twenty twenty-six brought its first non-stop flights to South America and the Middle East: Sao Paulo, and Abu Dhabi.
s4: More than seven million international travellers connect through Calgary every year, and never leave the airport.
What if a few of them stayed?
Every one percent who stay would mean seventy thousand more visitors.
It has already started. Since June twenty twenty-six, a stopover program lets travellers on two WestJet routes from the United Kingdom add up to seven days in Calgary, at no extra airfare.
s5: Calgary is also a base camp.
Banff National Park just set a record: four and a half million visitors in a single year.
And Calgary is its nearest international airport, about one hundred and thirty kilometres away.
Five UNESCO World Heritage Sites sit within a few hours' drive, along with the Badlands, dinosaur country, and Blackfoot heritage.
s6: And the city already knows how to draw a crowd.
The Calgary Stampede generated seven hundred and twenty-one million dollars across Alberta in twenty twenty-five, a third more than in twenty nineteen.
Meetings and conventions brought seventy-five thousand delegates, and two hundred and forty million dollars.
Sport, culture and major events added nearly one hundred and twenty-three million more.
s7: Other places have turned passing traffic into tourism.
Iceland offered a free stopover of up to seven days. Its visitor numbers roughly tripled in six years.
Singapore gives transit passengers a free city tour. More than eighty thousand took it in twenty nineteen.
Denver, another gateway to the Rockies, measured two hundred and nineteen dollars in visitor spending for every dollar of advertising.
And Dubai, with festivals all year round, fills almost eighty-one percent of its hotel rooms. Calgary fills sixty-seven and a half.
Not everything will carry over to Calgary. But the ideas have been tested.
s8: Tourism Calgary has set a target: double visitor spending, to six billion dollars, by twenty thirty-five.
That means growing about six percent, every year, for ten years.
Growth has costs too: crowding in Banff, and pressure on housing from short-term rentals. They need weighing alongside the gains.
s9: The room to grow is international.
These figures are the published estimates of Calgary's own tourism bodies, checked in November twenty twenty-six. See the full study at calgary insight dot c a.
